content: In low-resource countries, various interventions have been systematically reviewed to improve maternal and newborn health outcomes. Below is a detailed explanation of the findings and recommendations from these studies: 1. Emergency Obstetric Referral Interventions: A systematic review by Hussein et al. (2012) evaluated the effectiveness of emergency obstetric referral systems in developing countries. The study highlighted the importance of organized transport schemes and community involvement in improving access to skilled care during childbirth. 2. Community-Organized Transport Schemes: Community-organized transport systems, such as those using bicycles, ox carts, and canoes, were found to be effective in reducing delays in accessing healthcare facilities. These schemes were often supported by community surveillance systems and emergency funds. 3. Alternative Roles for Traditional Birth Attendants (TBAs): Integrating TBAs into formal health systems has shown potential to increase skilled birth attendance. Systematic reviews by Byrne and Morgan (2011) and Vieira et al. (2014) emphasized the importance of training TBAs to recognize danger signs and refer women to healthcare facilities. 4. Cultural Adaptation of Maternity Care Services: Studies have demonstrated that culturally appropriate maternity care models, such as those developed with indigenous communities, can increase the uptake of skilled care. For example, in Peru, a culturally tailored childbirth care model was co-designed with Quechua communities to address local needs. 5. Continuous Companionship During Labor and Birth: Continuous support for women during childbirth, as reviewed by Hodnett et al. (2011), has been shown to improve maternal satisfaction and reduce the need for medical interventions. This approach involves trained companions providing emotional and physical support throughout labor. 6. Community Mobilization Through Participatory Learning and Action Cycles: Women’s groups practicing participatory learning and action cycles have been effective in improving maternal and newborn health outcomes in low-resource settings. A systematic review by Prost et al. (2013) highlighted the role of these groups in increasing institutional births and skilled attendance. 7. Community Participation in Maternal Death Surveillance and Response: Community involvement in analyzing and disseminating information from maternal and perinatal death reviews has been recommended to improve accountability and healthcare quality. 8. Community Participation in Quality Improvement Processes: Engaging communities in quality improvement initiatives, such as monitoring healthcare services and providing feedback, has been shown to enhance service delivery and client satisfaction. 9. Community Participation in Program Planning and Implementation: 10. Male Involvement in Maternal Health: Interventions targeting male involvement, such as educating husbands on birth preparedness and emergency care, have been effective in improving maternal health outcomes. For example, in Pakistan, men were trained to support emergency transport and healthcare access for their wives. 11. Maternity Waiting Homes (MWHs): MWHs, located near healthcare facilities, provide temporary accommodation for high-risk pregnant women. These homes have been shown to reduce maternal and neonatal mortality by ensuring timely access to skilled care. 12. Behavior Change Communication and Community Mobilization: Participatory approaches, such as theater, songs, and community meetings, have been used to raise awareness about maternal health and promote behavior change. These interventions often include training healthcare workers and upgrading facilities to improve service quality. 13. Youth-Centered Participation: In Nepal, youth-centered interventions addressed sexual and reproductive health needs through community-driven action plans. These programs were designed based on extensive needs assessments and involved young people in the planning and implementation process. 14. Culturally Tailored Interventions for Minority Groups: Programs such as the Familias Sanas initiative in the USA bridged cultural gaps by employing bilingual, bicultural prenatal partners to provide education and support to Latina women. 15. Integrated Models of Care for Indigenous Communities: In Australia, collaboration with Indigenous communities led to the development of integrated antenatal care models, which included home visits, transportation, and culturally sensitive services. 16. Community-Based Health Worker Programs: In several countries, community health workers (CHWs) have been trained to deliver birth preparedness messages, conduct home visits, and provide postnatal care. These programs have been effective in increasing the use of skilled care and improving newborn health practices. 17. Social Mobilization Campaigns: Campaigns in countries like Honduras and Peru have used participatory community diagnosis and consensus-building strategies to address health issues and improve maternal and newborn care. 18. Evidence-Based Dialogue and Health Planning: In Kenya, evidence-based dialogue among healthcare providers, managers, and community representatives has been used to identify and address gaps in service delivery. 19. Gender and Health Equity Networks: In China, the Gender and Health Equity Network (GHEN) supported local health planning and increased women’s participation in decision-making processes. 20. Training and Capacity Building: Across various settings, training healthcare providers, TBAs, and community volunteers has been a key component of successful maternal health interventions. These efforts have focused on improving clinical skills, recognizing danger signs, and providing culturally appropriate care. Overall, these interventions demonstrate the importance of community involvement, cultural adaptation, and integrated approaches in improving maternal and newborn health outcomes in low-resource settings.
